WASHINGTON, May 11 (Reuters) - Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is not going to Beijing during President Donald Trump's trip to China this week, a person familiar with the matter said on Monday.
Huang was not invited, the source said, with the White House focusing more on agriculture and commercial aviation matters, such as orders for Boeing planes, on the current trip. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
A number of CEOs were expected to travel with Trump to help drum up business for U.S. companies, a top priority for his administration.
A person familiar with the matter confirmed last week that Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser was invited. Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon will attend as long as the trip goes ahead as planned, another source with knowledge of the matter said last week.
Trump has developed a strong relationship with Huang since he has been in office and agreed to allow the company's H200 AI chips to be exported to China. world-9b6cbbc692.headline: Qantas to outsource 850 local jobs with most roles moving to India
world-9b6cbbc692.fulltext:
Qantas to outsource 850 local jobs with most roles moving to India
- Published
Qantas will outsource 850 local corporate jobs to consulting giant Accenture with most roles moving to India as the airline fast-tracks AI investment.
In an internal email to staff on Tuesday, the Australian company's CEO Vanessa Hudson said "this is hard news for some and I'm sorry for the uncertainty it brings".
The job cuts will begin mid-2027, she said, and start with finance, procurement, people and marketing roles shifting "mostly" to teams in India and "some in Australia" as the firm seeks to modernise its IT systems.
Hudson said the "scale and speed of change in technology and AI is something none of us has seen in our lifetime", and it was in talks with unions and staff on the plans.
The move comes days after the airline provided a market update, flagging fare increases and flight cuts amid higher fuel costs.
On its new multi-year deal with Accenture, Hudson said it was about "modernising" the airline's IT systems to become "more efficient".
Qantas spends more than AU$1bn (US$691m; £514m) a year on technology, she said, and the company's back-end systems needed to be upgraded.
"Like every airline, we run on technology built up over decades for a different era, including more than 1,000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together," she said.
The deal with Accenture means "we will redesign and simplify parts of how our corporate functions work and reduce duplication", Hudson said, so staff can "spend more time on work that creates value for our customers and the business".
The company said that "in time", the work that Accenture takes over will be "transformed further with automation and AI".
Staff affected by the job cuts will be redeployed "where possible", the firm added, including new roles in Australia.
Qantas - which employs about 28,000 staff in Australia and another 4,000 globally - said thousands of its staff already use AI in their daily work.
The BBC has contacted the Australian Services Union for comment.

indian-startups-7c09294031.headline: Drone startup funding slumps in 2026
indian-startups-7c09294031.fulltext:
Drone startup funding slumps in 2026
India has the world's second-largest pool of defence-tech companies, but its share of investor backing lags
Share
A BMP tank moves past an Indian Navy's Mechanized Landing Craft as they participate in a tri-services military drill in Porbandar, Gujarat in November 2025 (Photo: Reuters)
The wars in Ukraine and West Asia have made drones a fixture of every serious arsenal, on battlefields that demand precision and mass at once, and where targets deep inside heavily defended airspace are struck again and again. 
India’s own experience during Operation Sindoor in May 2025 reinforced the point. The conflict showed the value of holding an adversary’s targets at risk from beyond its reach, and of fighting without bringing troops into contact. Since then, makers of unmanned aerial systems, most of them startups, have seen orders from the three services arrive far faster than before.
Data provided by Tracxn, a private market intelligence platform, and analysed by Blueprint show that 2025 also brought a sharp jump in the equity funding raised by India’s military and defence drone startups. Funding more than quadrupled to $159.2 million, a 343.1 per cent year-on-year rise, equal to about 90 per cent of the $176.3 million raised from 2020 to 2024 combined. In 2026, however, these startups have raised just $4.39 million up to October 5, 97.2 per cent less than in all of 2025. 
The founder of one of the sector’s larger startups, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the sharp fall in funding also reflected companies still absorbing the large sums raised the previous year, and perhaps the absence of any large player raising funds in 2026, likely because they had already done so in 2025. Deal activity has thinned too: according to the data, the number of funding rounds fell from 27 in 2025 to 11 in 2026 up to October 5. 
The pattern is sharper still among India’s pure-play military technology startups, those whose applications are primarily defence-specific, with no meaningful civilian or commercial use identified. According to the data, equity funding for these companies rose nearly sixfold in 2025 to $225.7 million, a 477.2 per cent year-on-year rise and about twice the $112.5 million raised from 2020 to 2024 combined. In 2026 up to October 5, however, they have raised just $5.22 million across seven funding rounds, against 18 the year before, 97.7 per cent less than in all of 2025.
 Dual-use technology startups, whose applications span both defence and civilian or commercial markets, tell a different story. Together with pure-play firms, they make up the whole of India’s military technology startups in the Tracxn data, and no company is counted in both groups. Their equity funding peaked at $90.9 million in 2024 and fell 37.5 per cent to $56.8 million in 2025, even as pure-play funding surged. But they have not slid as sharply in 2026: up to October 5, they have raised $48.2 million, 15.3 per cent less than in all of 2025. Over the same period, pure-play military and drone startups saw falls of 97.7 and 97.2 per cent, respectively.
 The 10 most-funded Indian military drone startups in the Tracxn data are, in order, Raphe, ideaForge, Garuda Aerospace, Vayudh, Anadrone, EndureAir Systems, S4E, BonV Aero, IG Defence and Aeroarc. Together they have raised $322.4 million, with Raphe alone accounting for $154 million, or 47.8 per cent. Uttar Pradesh is home to three of them (Raphe, EndureAir Systems and IG Defence), more than any other state on the list. Maharashtra and Delhi have two each, while Tamil Nadu, Haryana and Odisha have one apiece. The three Uttar Pradesh firms account for about 53 per cent of the group’s total, though about 90 per cent of that is Raphe’s.
 Tracxn’s September 2026 report on military technology tracks 3,224 companies worldwide that supply technology to armed forces, from makers of unmanned weapons systems to firms providing training simulators and medical technology. Of these, 416 were founded in India, the second-highest number after the US, with 1,215. India also ranks second by the number of companies that have raised funding: 109, against 270 for the US. But measured as a share, India does less well. Only about one in four Indian companies (26 per cent) have raised funding. In France, the figure is 42 per cent; in Turkiye, 38 per cent; in Israel, 36 per cent; and in China, 29 per cent. Among the eight countries with the most military technology companies, India ranks fifth on this measure, ahead only of Canada (24 per cent), the United Kingdom (23 per cent) and the US (22 per cent).
 As military technology startups, including those working on unmanned systems, compete for a share of India’s growing defence procurement, experts have raised concerns about whether they get enough support to cross the “valley of death”. This is the stage at which a startup that has made progress in research and development, or built a prototype, runs short of funds to take the next step, such as commercial production. The question is how this gap can be addressed.

climate-energy-e01a30f2fa.headline: Analysis: Fossil-fuel CO2 emissions set to dip in 2026 as Iran conflict hits oil use

Analysis: Fossil-fuel CO2 emissions set to dip in 2026 as Iran conflict hits oil use
Carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels and cement are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026 to 38.2bn tonnes of CO2 (GtCO2), according to new figures from the Global Carbon Project.
This guest post is by:
- Dr Zeke Hausfather, Carbon Brief’s climate science contributor
- Prof Pierre Friedlingstein, chair of mathematical modelling of climate systems at the University of Exeter and part of the Global Carbon Project team.
Carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from fossil fuels and cement are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026 to 38.2bn tonnes of CO2 (GtCO2), according to new figures from the Global Carbon Project.
The 21st edition of the annual “global carbon budget” report, published today, says that this small decline is largely due to a 1.9% drop in emissions from oil and the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict and the closure of the strait of Hormuz.
Emissions from coal continue to increase slightly.
The Global Carbon Project’s projections for fossil fuel and cement CO2 emissions in 2026 are preliminary, with a range that spans a fall of -1.5% to a rise of +0.6%.
This means a small increase in emissions can not be ruled out.
Emissions from land-use change, such as deforestation, are projected to rise in 2026.
This is primarily driven by peat fires and forest degradation in south-east Asia and is linked to the development of a strong El Niño event this year.
As a result, total CO2 emissions from fossil fuels and land use are projected to reach a record high of 43.3GtCO2 in 2026 – marginally above 42.8GtCO2 in 2025.
Research published alongside the report by the same team in Nature Climate Change finds that the growth in solar, wind and electric vehicles (EVs) now offsets around two-thirds of the emissions that would otherwise come from rising energy demand.
However, the deployment of these technologies is not yet enough to push global emissions into a sustained decline, according to the study.
The 2026 global carbon budget report also estimates that:
- Fossil emissions are projected to fall in China (-0.9%), the US (-1.3%) and the EU (-1.5%) in 2026, but rise by 4.4% in India.
- Oil emissions are projected to fall in every major region, with the largest drop in China (-4.6%).
- Land-use emissions averaged 4.9GtCO2 per year over 2016-25, around 21% lower than the decade before.
- Total CO2 emissions (fossil and land-use) grew by an average 0.3% per year over the past decade (2016-25), compared with 1.7% per year over the decade before.
- The remaining carbon budget to limit warming to 1.5C is 150GtCO2, or less than four years of current emissions.
- The land sink in 2025 was the highest on record, rebounding after being weakened during the 2023-24 El Niño. The current El Niño is expected to weaken the land sink in 2027.
- The concentration of CO2 in the atmosphere is set to reach 427.7 parts per million (ppm) in 2026, 54% above pre-industrial levels.
(For more on previous editions of the Global Carbon Project’s annual report, see Carbon Brief’s coverage in 2025, 2024, 2023 and 2022.)
Total emissions edge up as land-use emissions rise
Total global CO2 emissions, which combines fossil fuels and land-use change, are projected to reach a record high of 43.3GtCO2 in 2026, up from 42.8GtCO2 in 2025.
The increase in 2026 comes entirely from a projected rise in land-use emissions, which are more challenging to estimate than fossil emissions.
(The global carbon budget groups emissions from fossil fuels and cement production as “fossil emissions”. Carbon Brief follows this convention throughout this piece.)
If land-use emissions had stayed at 2025 levels, total emissions would have fallen slightly in 2026 to around 42.6GtCO2.
Each edition of the global carbon budget updates the historical record as new data and methods become available. The chart below shows total emissions in this year’s budget compared with the five previous editions.
This year’s estimates of historical fossil emissions are around 0.3GtCO2 per year higher than in last year’s budget.
This is largely because the report now estimates a smaller “cement carbonation” sink in the wake of research published this year in Communications Sustainability. In other words, it estimates that cement is able to slowly reabsorb less CO2 over its lifetime than previously thought.
Estimates of land-use emissions have also been revised, including a spike in 2018 – visible in the chart above – linked to updated cropland data for Colombia.
The updated numbers show that total emissions have grown by 0.3% per year over the past decade (2016-25), compared with 1.7% per year over 2006-15.
Fossil emissions grew about 0.9% per year in the past decade, compared with 1.9% the decade before. Over the same period, land-use emissions have declined.
While the slowdown reflects real progress, a plateau in emissions is still a long way from the rapid declines needed to reach net-zero emissions and stabilise global temperatures.
With human-caused warming reaching 1.37C above pre-industrial levels (1850-1900) in 2025, the report estimates that the remaining carbon budget to limit warming to 1.5C, with a 50% chance, is 150GtCO2 from the start of 2027. That is less than four years of 2026 emissions.
Meanwhile, the budgets for 1.7C and 2C are 510GtCO2 and 1,035GtCO2, respectively – or around 12 and 24 years of current emissions.
Fossil emissions made up around 88% of total CO2 emissions over the past decade, with land-use change making up the remaining 12%.
This is a marked change from the first half of the 20th century, when land-use emissions were larger than those from fossil fuels.
The figure below shows global emissions, split into fossil and land-use components.
Global per-capita fossil emissions peaked in the early 2010s and have since slightly declined. At around 4.6 tonnes per person in 2026, they are about 4% below that peak.
It is worth noting that this global average hides very large differences between countries. For example, 2025 per-capita emissions in India are only 2.2 tonnes, compared with 14.5 tonnes in the US.
Land-use emissions rise in 2026
Land-use emissions come from deforestation, forest degradation, wood harvest, peatland drainage and fires. They are partly offset by forest regrowth and new forests.
Net land-use emissions averaged 4.9GtCO2 per year over 2016-25, down from 6.2GtCO2 per year over 2006-15, marking a decline of around 21%. This decline holds across all three of the “bookkeeping” models used by the Global Carbon Project to track land-use emissions.
(For more on trends in global land-use emissions and how they are calculated, see Carbon Brief’s explainer.)
Land-use emissions are projected to rise to 5.1GtCO2 in 2026, up from 4.4GtCO2 in 2025.
The report attributes the increase to peat fires, almost all ignited by people, and forest degradation in south-east Asia due to drier conditions associated with El Niño.
Uncertainties in land-use emissions are much higher than for fossil emissions given the challenges in tracking them.
While 2026 shows a nominal increase, it is only slightly above the average over the past decade.
Brazil, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Indonesia together accounted for 2.6GtCO2 of land-use emissions per year over 2015-25, or around 54% of the global total.
The figure below shows how land-use emissions for these three countries and the rest of the world have changed since 1960.
Fossil emissions fall in most major economies
Global fossil CO2 emissions are projected to fall by around 0.4% in 2026. However, challenges associated with precisely measuring and projecting 2026 means this could end up anywhere between a 1.5% decline and a 0.6% increase.
The figure below provides a breakdown of fossil emissions over time by major country and region, including China, the US, the EU, India and the rest of the world.
The global carbon budget report sets out the following projections for 2026 in major economies:
The figure below shows how each country or region contributed to changes in global fossil emissions in each year between 2023 and 2026.
A growing number of countries are cutting emissions while growing their economies.
The report finds that 40 countries, together accounting for 26% of global fossil emissions, significantly reduced their emissions while their economies grew over 2016-25. This compares with 22 countries in the previous decade.
Oil emissions fall as coal emissions slightly increase
Coal accounts for around 41% of global fossil CO2 emissions in 2026, oil 33% and gas 21%. Cement accounts for around 2%, after the carbonation sink is subtracted.
Oil is the main driver of the decline in global fossil emissions in 2026. Oil emissions are projected to fall by 1.9% (with a range of -2.6% to -1.2%), or 243m tonnes of CO2 (MtCO2).
The left panel of the figure below shows that this is one of the largest annual falls in the record, with the exception of 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic. Other large declines occurred during the global financial crisis in 2009 and in the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1992.
The chart on the right shows how oil emissions are projected to fall in every major region in 2026.
The global carbon budget links most of the oil decline to higher prices and reductions in output after the Iran conflict resulted in the closure of the strait of Hormuz.
Petrol and diesel prices in the US, China and EU were 10-50% higher than in 2025, depending on the fuel and the period.
A study published in parallel by the team behind the global carbon budget reveals that growth in EVs accounted for around a fifth of the overall drop in oil emissions in 2026.
This is consistent with Carbon Brief analysis published in September that estimated that global fossil-fuel emissions were set to fall in 2026 amid the Hormuz crisis.
By contrast, coal emissions are projected to rise by 0.6% (-0.6% to +1.7%), with a strong increase in emissions in India partly offset by sharp falls in the EU and US.
Gas emissions, meanwhile, are projected to fall by 0.3% (-1.6% to +0.9%) – making them effectively flat.
The figure below shows global emissions by fuel since 1959.
Coal emissions grew rapidly in the 2000s, at around 4% per year, but have risen only slightly since 2013. Even with continued growth, 2026 coal emissions are only around 6% above their 2013 level.
Oil emissions remain about 1% above their pre-pandemic level in 2019.
The figure below shows the contribution of each fuel to the change in global emissions between 2023 and 2026.
Land sink in 2025 is highest on record
The annual global carbon budget report tracks both the sources of CO2, from fossil fuels and land use, as well as the “sinks” that take it up: the ocean, the land and the atmosphere.
Over 2016-25, the ocean took up around 27% of total emissions, or 11.1GtCO2 per year, whereas the land around 22%, or 9.2GtCO2 per year. The remaining 48% accumulated in the atmosphere.
The figure below shows the sources of emissions (above zero) and where they end up (below zero) each year. The sum of the sinks is shown as a dashed line for comparison with total emissions.
The Global Carbon Project estimates that the land sink in 2025 was the highest on record, at around 13.3GtCO2 – 50% larger than in 2024.
This reflects a strong recovery in the tropics after the 2023-24 El Niño had suppressed the land sink, along with gradual growth of the sink associated with higher atmospheric CO2 concentrations.
The carbon budget does not always balance. In 2024, the estimated sinks exceeded the estimated sources by 6.7GtCO2, the largest “imbalance” on record. This partly offset an imbalance in the opposite direction in 2023 of 3.3GtCO2.

MakeMyTrip's India arm gets Sebi nod to float IPO
The proceeds from the planned IPO will be utilised by MakeMyTrip for long term growth, inorganic opportunities and repurchase of different types shares
Nasdaq-listed travel booking platform MakeMyTrip's India subsidiary has received Sebi's approval to launch an initial public offering (IPO), according to an update available on the markets regulator's website.
MakeMyTrip (India) Ltd (MMT India) had filed draft papers with Sebi in July through the confidential route. After examining the draft documents, the regulator issued its final observations on November 6.
Sebi's observations mark an important step in the IPO process, allowing the company to proceed with preparations for its public issues, subject to applicable regulatory requirements.
The proposed IPO is expected to comprise a sale of equity shares in MMT India by its parent MakeMyTrip and its wholly-owned subsidiary, ibibo Group Holdings (Singapore) Pte Ltd, the Gurugram-headquartered company said in a regulatory filing with Nasdaq.
Following the completion of the proposed IPO, MMT India will continue to remain a subsidiary of MakeMyTrip, with its financial results continuing to be consolidated with those of the parent company, it had said.
"MakeMyTrip expects the proposed initial public offering and listing of MMT India to enhance its brand visibility and support MMT India's ability to incentivise and promote talent in a competitive technology recruitment landscape," the filing stated.
The net proceeds received by MakeMyTrip and ibibo Group Holdings from the sale of shares in MMT India are expected to strengthen the parent's cash position.
The proceeds will be utilised for long-term growth, strategic inorganic initiatives and repurchases of different classes of securities, including convertible securities, by MakeMyTrip, the filing stated.
MakeMyTrip swung back into profit for the three months ending September, 2026 boosted by increased booking across all categories. The company reported a net profit of $1.8 million for the second quarter of FY27 as compared to loss of $5.7 million in the similar period a year ago. The revenue for the second quarter touched $235.2 million which was a 11.2% increase when compared to the similar period of last fiscal.

The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
Big Tech sees a culture war over progress. But the real fault line is electricity: drawing it from the grid and generating it onsite provoke different kinds of backlash, neither easily solved by public relations.
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.
As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape.
Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ.
It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words.
But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.
Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.
One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables).
The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport.
Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity.
Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.
Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand.
The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company.
Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid.
But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out).
The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.
Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency).
Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do. But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation?
Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that.
But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something.
So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin, where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.
But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

deep-tech-a42e59890a.headline: A laser that shoots down drones for a fraction of the cost: How close is India to deploying it?
deep-tech-a42e59890a.fulltext:
Drones have turned air defence into a question of arithmetic, upending traditional calculations of the cost of warfare. Drones costing a few thousand dollars each can be launched in large numbers to scout, locate air-defence positions and attack installations. This could lead to a situation in which a defender who responds to each one with a missile runs out of interceptors long before the attacker runs out of drones. That is why high-energy lasers, which promise to engage targets at the speed of light and at a fraction of the cost per shot, have attracted so much interest from militaries across the world.
India is now moving its indigenous Directed-Energy Weapon (DEW) programme from technology demonstrations towards industrial production. The harder question is whether a successful trial can translate into a dependable battlefield capability.
How does a laser weapon work?
A laser weapon works by directing a concentrated beam at a vulnerable part of a target, such as its airframe, engine, battery or control system. The sustained energy generates heat that weakens the structure or disables critical components. At lower power, the beam can dazzle or damage a drone's optical sensors.
Many components need to come together to make a laser weaoncome together as an effective combat tool. 
The beam is only one part of the system. It also needs sensors to detect and classify the target, a tracker to follow it, beam-control optics to hold the aimpoint on a small moving object, as well as power and cooling equipment. Artificial intelligence can help with classification, tracking and selecting a vulnerable section to target.
The attraction of lasers
The cost-effectiveness and unlimited magazine depth of directed energy weapons are key to the rising interest in these systems. 
The main attraction of these weapons is the cost per engagement, as a laser weapon does not consume missiles, shells or bullets to bring down a single drone. Its marginal cost is mainly the electricity or fuel needed to power it. US defence estimates have put the energy cost of some engagements at around $1 to $10. This, however, excludes the cost of buying, maintaining and operating the complete system.
Lasers also offer greater magazine depth. A missile launcher has a fixed number of interceptors, while a laser can keep firing as long as power and cooling allow. That does not mean it can destroy every target instantly. Each engagement requires target acquisition, tracking and sufficient dwell time on the target. Overheating can also limit the duration of an engagement.
Directed-energy weapons belong to the next generation of weapon systems. They hold considerable promise but also have serious limitations in their employment. Their effectiveness in conclusively destroying targets has not yet been established, while their cost-effectiveness remains low. As a result, despite considerable discussion about their battlefield utility, their adoption remains limited. Directed-energy weapon technologies are still around five to 10 years away from maturing into practical battlefield capabilities.
Lt Gen PR Shankar (retired), Professor, Aerospace Dept IIT Madras and former DG Artillery
Where India stands
India's most important progress has come from the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO). In April 2025, it demonstrated its vehicle-mounted MK-II(A) laser DEW at the National Open Air Range in Kurnool, Andhra Pradesh. Developed by the Centre for High Energy Systems and Sciences (CHESS), the system engaged fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), countered a multiple-drone attack and damaged surveillance sensors and antennae.
The DRDO and its establishment, CHESS, are developing lasers of different classes for the country. 
The 30-kilowatt system is designed to counter drone swarms, fixed-wing UAVs and surveillance sensors at ranges of up to 5 km, and its final trials were completed in August 2025. In September, DRDO said it would issue an expression of interest within six months to select an industry partner for a first-of-production model. That marks a move from technology demonstrator towards production, but does not mean the weapon has been inducted or is available in significant numbers.
Various systems in this family of weapons are at different stages of development. The 2-kilowatt weapon is reported to be in production, with Adani Defence and Aerospace, Astra Microwave Products and Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) as industry participants. Earlier systems are reported to have been used by all three armed services. Numbers delivered and deployment details are not public.
The 10-kilowatt system, meant to engage drones at around 1.5 to 2 km, has reportedly received Acceptance of Necessity, with BEL and Larsen & Toubro as development-cum-production partners. However, the first production models were still awaited as of September 2025. Claims that a 10-kilowatt system was used during Operation Sindoor are conflicting and need independent confirmation.
Higher-power systems, including the 50- and 100-kilowatt classes under DURGA-II (Directionally Unrestricted Ray-Gun Array) and a reported 300-kilowatt ambition called Surya, remain development goals.
In August 2025, DRDO also carried out the maiden trial of its Integrated Air Defence Weapon System (IADWS) off the Odisha coast. It combines the Quick Reaction Surface-to-Air Missile, the Very Short Range Air Defence System and a high-power laser DEW under a unified command network. During the trial, the three components collectively engaged and destroyed three targets: two high-speed fixed-wing UAVs and a multicopter drone.
DRDO has also begun work on a laser pod for helicopters such as the Dhruv and its armed variant, Rudra, with development reportedly targeted for completion by the end of 2029. For now, it remains under development. Mounting a laser on an aircraft brings challenges involving weight, power, cooling, vibration and aerodynamics.
Apart from India, many other countries are also working on similar weapons for their own armed forces. 
India is not alone in developing this class of directed-energy weapons. Israel delivered its first Iron Beam system to its armed forces in December 2025. Britain awarded a £316 million contract in November 2025 for the DragonFire naval laser. The US Navy has fitted the HELIOS system on the destroyer USS Preble, Germany is developing an airborne laser demonstrator, and China has showcased systems such as Silent Hunter and LY-1.
The limits of a laser
Several constraints can limit the effectiveness of this type of weapon in actual combat. Fog, rain, dust, smoke and clouds can absorb or scatter the beam. A system that performs well in clear-weather trials may have a shorter effective range in poor conditions, a problem that can be particularly severe in dusty deserts, maritime environments and high-altitude areas with cloud cover.
A beam also needs a clear line of sight, so low-flying drones behind hills or buildings are difficult to engage. Dwell time is another issue. Against a swarm, the seconds spent on one drone are seconds not spent on the next. An adversary could also use heat-resistant materials or manoeuvres to buy time.
Power and cooling add further limits on size, weight and mobility, especially when these systems are mounted on helicopters.
For the armed forces, the first uses are likely to involve protecting airfields, bases, radars, ammunition depots and forward formations against drones and loitering munitions. Along the Line of Control and the Line of Actual Control, much will depend on whether the systems work reliably in difficult weather and terrain, remain mobile and integrate with existing radar and air-defence networks.
Lasers are unlikely to replace guns and missiles, especially against ballistic missiles and high-speed cruise missiles.
India has demonstrated its ability to develop and use high-energy lasers against aerial targets, but its systems are at very different levels of maturity. The next test is whether DRDO and industry can manufacture reliable systems in sufficient numbers and demonstrate that they can perform during prolonged operations, bad weather and saturation attacks.
Readiness can only be proven under operational conditions.

india-deep-tech-9d8b20a654.headline: ‘Bad Decision’: Ex-IAF Chief Slams HAL For Bypassing Local Uttam Radar On Tejas Mk1A
india-deep-tech-9d8b20a654.fulltext:
# Ex-IAF Chief Bhadauria Blasts HAL Radar Choice As ‘Bad Decision’, Unpacks Tejas Mk2 & AMCA Roadmap
In a strikingly direct assessment of India’s indigenous military aviation ecosystem, former Chief of the Air Staff Air Chief Marshal R.K.S. Bhadauria (Retd) has termed state-run airframer Hindustan Aeronautics Limited’s (HAL) choice to bypass the homegrown Uttam AESA radar in favour of additional Israeli radars for the Tejas LCA Mk1A a “bad decision.”
Speaking on the NDTV Ctrl+Alt+Defence podcast co-hosted by Livefist founder Shiv Aroor, ACM Bhadauria outlined a detailed critique of institutional bottlenecks within HAL, revealed developmental hitches surrounding the LCA Mk2’s undercarriage, and provided critical context on the forward momentum of India’s 5th-generation Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) program now that private sector bids are formally in.
ACM Bhadauria expressed sharp disappointment over what he characterised as HAL’s reluctance to commit aggressively to the indigenous Uttam Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) radar, developed by DRDO’s Electronics and Radar Development Establishment (LRDE). Despite trial data confirming that the indigenous sensor surpasses the performance of imported alternatives, HAL recently opted to procure further tranches of the Israeli EL/M-2052 AESA radar for the LCA Mk1A fleet.
“I hear that HAL has gone in for more of the same radar and not taken Uttam, which is a bad decision to my mind, because even if it means a little delay, in any case the aircraft itself has got delayed,” Bhadauria stated. “What delay are we talking of that ‘radar integration is delaying me 1 year, 1 and a half year’? That is the importance we need to give to the indigenous system.”
He emphasized that the Uttam radar has fully matured and earned its operational credentials: “I am aware of Uttam. I think Uttam has already come of age. It is already ready for induction, integration onto the aircraft.” He further noted that flight test data gathered by the National Flight Test Centre (NFTC) proved its technological superiority: “It is already giving more range than the radar that we are already integrating on 1A.”
Addressing why HAL chose to stick with foreign hardware, Bhadauria pointed out a systemic preference for ease over enterprise. “At times they just pick up from abroad because it is easier to certify, it is faster, there are no risks involved,” he noted, adding candidly: “HAL already was co-producing that other radar. That would have been their larger interest, I would say to put it very bluntly, more than anything else.”
Turning to the medium-weight LCA Mk2 program, Bhadauria offered fresh detail on what has slowed down the prototype’s timeline, pointing specifically to landing gear development issues.
“From where they are now, there’s been some delay. I think some of the delay was undercarriage related. They got into some problem,” Bhadauria revealed.
While acknowledging that design and development (D&D) challenges are par for the course in complex fighter jet engineering, he called for accelerated work routines and advanced testing methodologies to recover lost ground. “D&D delays we have to give it to HAL, but I also want HAL and everybody involved in this to move much, much faster,” he said.
He urged the development agency and HAL to aggressively compress the flight-test schedule using modern digital tools. “There is a huge case for using technology and particularly AI-enabled technology for compressing all our plans of the future. I don’t think we are seriously working there. If you get all this into it, I think we’ll hack it.”
ACM Bhadauria did not pull punches when evaluating HAL’s broader corporate ethos, project management track record, and reinvestment culture. He highlighted an urgent need to break out of rigid public-sector routines:
“Project management has been disastrous at HAL… If you expect government organizations to manufacture and be as efficient as private, it will never happen.”
Recalling earlier efforts to establish a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) for the stealth AMCA project, he explained that the initiative failed because HAL insisted on dominant control. “If you keep HAL as the majority, it is same procedure, same sense, your control remains same… It was not a lack of interest from the private sector; it was lack of interest for the terms and for the kind of combination that was presented to them.”
Addressing HAL’s exclusion from the ongoing private-led AMCA manufacturing bidding process, Bhadauria confirmed that HAL’s proposal stumbled on basic compliance. “One of the partners did not meet the technical criteria. The criteria that the partners were to meet, those criteria were not met.”
Defence Secretary R.K. Singh had revealed this on a previous episode of the same podcast recorded at the NDTV Defence Summit.
Criticizing HAL’s sluggish pace on futuristic technologies like the CATS (Combat Air Teaming System) Warrior CCA, Bhadauria underscored a chronic lack of internal R&D funding. “If you just see how much money our DPSUs are putting in research, it’s bare minimum. There’s no reason they should have not been putting 15 odd percent into research.”
Calling out the lack of round-the-clock intensity at manufacturing units, he remarked: “We need to work three shifts. I keep saying I never see lights on at night. That means we are not working. If you think that in one, one-and-a-half shift you will change the scene in this country, it won’t happen.”
With private sector consortium bids now formally submitted for the execution of India’s 5th-generation AMCA prototype phase, Bhadauria framed the development as a crucial inflection point for national aerospace.
He dismissed suggestions that the target timelines are unachievable, noting that industrial capability within India has matured significantly over the past decade. The primary task now, he noted, is executing contracts swiftly and ensuring that state machinery actively supports the winning private entity.
“Now is the start point that we should worry about and see that there are no delays from now. I don’t see any reason why we should now slip on times,” Bhadauria asserted. “Once this kind of contract and this kind of attention is given, whoever is chosen, he will deliver. But I must also say that there will be a lot of support that is required across the board.”
He highlighted that certification agencies and government institutions must adjust their operational mindset to work seamlessly with private defence partners: “There’s a lack of proactive action in terms of certification agencies dealing with private sector. The way they deal with DPSUs is different than the way they deal with private sector. These are all ground realities. So we have to grow out of it.”
Despite his detailed critique of past missteps, the former Air Chief emphasized that the defence establishment cannot afford to remain bogged down in historical recriminations or inter-agency friction.
Refusing to assign single-point blame for historical delays, Bhadauria insisted on collective accountability and a unified push forward. “We should go beyond blame games. I think we all have a hand in this because we all had responsibilities. If we had moved faster, found a way to sort out the issues, we would have been faster.”
“The delays are past us and we shouldn’t worry too much about what has happened. We should at least now get it right,” Bhadauria concluded. “It has to be about a national will to move these things forward… National will, and then putting our contracts with our own industry and having full faith in it and everybody in the chain supports it. I don’t see any reason why we cannot succeed.”

     Paras Semiconductors partners with US firm BroadPak to develop advanced packaging facility in India
Paras Semiconductors, a subsidiary of Paras Defence and Space Technologies, has announced a technology partnership with US-based BroadPak Corporation to develop advanced semiconductor packaging capabilities in India, according to a release on Monday.
Through the tie-up, Paras Semiconductors aims to set up an advanced heterogeneous integration and 3D packaging OSAT (outsourced semiconductor assembly and test) facility in the country.

The two firms will also explore joint development of packaging platforms for AI and high-performance computing applications, and collaborate on training Indian engineers.
BroadPak, headquartered in San Jose, California, was founded in 2007 and brings specialised expertise across advanced packaging design, manufacturing and system integration, according to the release.
“Our entry into the semiconductor sector represents a strategic expansion into a technology domain that is increasingly critical to India’s AI and data centres and industrial capabilities,” Munjal Sharad Shah, Managing Director, Paras Defence and Space Technologies, said.
Paras Semiconductors CEO Santosh Kumar said the company intends to build a packaging platform that can address the performance, connectivity and thermal needs of next-generation applications.
BroadPak Founder and CEO Farhang Yazdani noted India’s growing semiconductor ecosystem offered an important opportunity to develop capabilities in heterogeneous integration and system-level packaging.

Zipline has raised $1.5 billion and ramped up its partnership with Walmart, a pair of deals that have raised the autonomous drone delivery and logistics startup’s profile and valuation.
Zipline and Walmart reached a new multi-year agreement to add 300 drone delivery sites across the United States. The two companies have had a drone delivery agreement since 2021, but this deal is a significant jump from the 21 active drone delivery sites they have together today.
On the fundraising side, Zipline’s $1.5 billion raise was led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global, with participation from Valor Equity Partners, Fidelity Management & Research Company, Uber, Tiger Global, J.P. Morgan, ARK Invest, and Salesforce Ventures. Zipline is now valued at $21.5 billion.
The company, which has developed a drone delivery ecosystem that includes aircraft, launch and landing systems, and logistics software, said it plans to use the funds to expand its U.S. manufacturing facilities and hire more workers to build out a nationwide drone delivery network.
Founded in 2014, Zipline got its start in Africa, where it used its autonomous drones to deliver blood in Rwanda, and later expanded to Ghana and Nigeria. The California-based company began its first operations in the U.S. in 2020, ferrying medical equipment and supplies to Novant Health in North Carolina. The following year, it struck a deal with Walmart.
But it was in 2022 that Zipline’s business really started to take off in the United States. Zipline received its Part 135 air carrier certification from the Federal Aviation Administration that year, a critical regulatory hurdle that authorized the company to complete long-range commercial drone deliveries. It has locked in a number of partnerships since then, including with Uber earlier this year.
Zipline now uses its drones to deliver food, retail, agricultural, and health products in five African countries, several cities in the United States, and Japan. Zipline’s home delivery service uses Zipline’s Platform 2 drones, which are designed to carry up to eight pounds and travel to customers within a 10-mile radius. Its larger Platform 1 drones are used for long-range deliveries for enterprise, business, and government that can cover 120 miles round trip.
The company said Thursday that its share of delivery revenue grew from 10.8% to 34.9% between March and October of this year. This latest funding aims to push that metric even higher.

Edtech company PhysicsWallah is using artificial intelligence (AI) to improve operational efficiencies and reduce its workforce requirements, even as it looks to expand through inorganic route — acquisitions. The Noida-based company also continues to face profitability challenges in its offline business, despite the expansion of its Vidyapeeth centres.
During its Q2 FY27 earnings call, management confirmed that its total employee count, which stood at around 19,100, and faculty strength of approximately 7,100 declined sequentially in the quarter. The firm attributed the reduction partly to efficiencies from AI across content creation, quality checks, test paper preparation and evaluation.
Management said AI now writes around 90% of the company's code. The shift towards automation has also helped contain employee expenses, which declined 2.3% year-on-year in Q2 FY27, excluding ESOP costs. For the first half of FY27, employee expenses were down 2.4% compared to the same period last year.
However, PhysicsWallah continues to invest in technology which stood at Rs 104 crore in H1 FY27, compared to Rs 70 crore in the corresponding period last year.
While AI-led efficiencies have helped improve operating leverage, PhysicsWallah's offline business remains a key area to watch. The segment reported a pre-Ind AS EBITDA loss of Rs 108 crore in H1 FY27, compared to Rs 120 crore in the year-ago period, as per figures discussed during the call.
The offline business reported 9% year-on-year revenue growth to Rs 541 crore in Q2 FY27, while H1 revenue rose 12% to Rs 1,031 crore. Management attributed the moderation in growth partly to lower NEET enrolments and delays in government exam notifications, which affected demand at some of its centres.
PhysicsWallah operates 370 offline centres, including 167 Vidyapeeth centres, compared to 117 in the previous year. Vidyapeeth contributed around 66% of the company's offline business collections in H1 FY27. Management said the standalone Vidyapeeth business is already profitable and expects the broader offline segment to move closer to breakeven. The company plans to add 25-30 offline centres annually over the next two to three years, while keeping a tighter check on upfront costs.
Alongside its focus on operational efficiency, PhysicsWallah is also evaluating acquisitions to expand its online education biz. The company said it is in advanced discussions with a couple of fully online education businesses and is actively evaluating several other opportunities.
It has earmarked less than $20 million for these acquisitions, in line with the Rs 300 crore allocation from its IPO proceeds for unidentified acquisitions. Management expects the deals to be margin-accretive and said they could strengthen its presence in new categories while offering synergies with its technology and YouTube-led distribution.
PhysicsWallah's FY27 revenue growth guidance of around 30% includes the potential contribution from acquisitions. However, management expects M&A to contribute less than 5% to revenue growth during the year.
The company reported consolidated revenue of Rs 1,242 crore in Q2 FY27, which rose 18% year-on-year, while net profit rose to Rs 142 crore from Rs 70 crore in the year-ago quarter.

indian-startups-25ea5b9e4a.headline: Chinese AI firms want Silicon Valley’s top minds. Poaching them won’t be easy
indian-startups-25ea5b9e4a.fulltext:
Chinese AI companies are hiring Silicon Valley-based engineers to work on their models, potentially tapping into the talent at American labs like OpenAI and Anthropic.
MiniMax, the Hong Kong-listed Chinese AI startup, currently has around 16 San Francisco-based job openings listed on its website, including for a research lead focused on developing its core AI model. The company is also recruiting specialists in finance, law, life sciences, and cybersecurity, as well as a lead recruiter to attract top AI talent in Silicon Valley and Seattle.
Moonshot AI, the Chinese company behind the Kimi AI model, is looking for U.S.-based “solutions architects,” who will “help enterprise customers integrate its AI models into their businesses.”
American AI companies, with their deep pockets, have attracted global talent, including many Chinese engineers, by offering high compensation and opportunities to work on the world’s best models. In comparison, Chinese companies have so far largely relied on homegrown talent. Hiring in the U.S. reflects a strategic shift by Chinese companies as they look to compete and stay close to one of their most lucrative markets, experts said.
“Wanting to establish research teams in Silicon Valley makes perfect sense for Chinese AI companies seeking access to talent and the latest developments in the industry,” Cheryl Wu, a researcher in the economics of AI at Yale University and global think tank GovAI, told Rest of World.
Good Work and $$$
More than half of the world’s top AI researchers complete their undergraduate studies in China, a September study by research center Carnegie China said, based on the educational backgrounds of people who published papers at NeurIPS, one of the world’s leading AI conferences.
Yet the U.S. remains a global magnet for AI talent, the study concluded.
In 2025, the U.S. saw a net gain of 2,145 researchers while China recorded a net loss of 1,729, according to the analysis.
China’s AI companies have been trying to lure top Chinese researchers at American AI labs to return home. One high-profile example is Tencent, which recruited former OpenAI researcher Yao Shunyu to lead its AI research.
Chinese companies are seeking “little geniuses” who have worked at companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, a headhunter recruiting for Chinese labs in the Bay Area told Rest of World, requesting anonymity as she is not authorized to speak to the media.
These attempts, however, have not had much success because Chinese companies often struggle to match the salaries paid by their Silicon Valley peers.
“It’s money. Chinese companies simply don’t have enough of it to offer competitive wages for talent,” said Wu, who published a report examining Chinese AI companies’ financing with research institute Epoch AI. “They have only recently begun raising more substantial funding and still lag far behind their U.S. competitors.”
There is a stark gap between what Chinese and American AI companies pay employees.
MiniMax spent $84.3 million on employee remuneration in 2025, equivalent to roughly $203,000 per person, based on its year-end head count of 415, according to its financial filings. The annualized remuneration costs of Z.AI, another Hong Kong-listed Chinese AI lab, in the first half of 2026 amounted to $140,000 per employee. Neither company disclosed a breakdown of pay for engineers or researchers, and both figures include share-based compensation and staff across all departments.
In comparison, OpenAI advertises annual base salaries of $250,000 to $445,000 for research engineers in San Francisco, before equity awards. Three Chinese researchers working in Silicon Valley say it’s common for their peers to get an annual compensation package worth more than $1 million.
As of September, China’s six leading AI firms collectively generated only about 10% of the combined AI-related revenue of OpenAI and Anthropic, according to Wu’s research.
“Career prospects are another factor. Even senior Meta engineers might accept a lower-ranking position to join Anthropic because of its work on frontier AI,” Wu said. “That makes it even harder to persuade top talent to join a lab whose models are just not at the cutting edge.”
Chinese tech companies are now ramping up their salary game. If an AI researcher had offers from OpenAI or Anthropic, ByteDance’s frontier model division Seed would try to lure them with a competing offer that’s 1.5 times higher, according to a person familiar with the team.
Wu Yonghui, a veteran AI researcher who worked at Google for 17 years, joined Seed as the head of research in early 2025. Seed currently lists 71 positions in San Jose, San Diego, and Seattle.
But even with matching pay, three Chinese researchers working in the U.S. told Rest of World they preferred American companies for better work-life balance and the chance to work on frontier models.
“I think most of the top Chinese talent would feel pretty comfortable in Silicon Valley; it’s the only other place where “996” isn’t really frowned upon,” Damien Ma, director of Carnegie China, told Rest of World, referring to the demanding work culture common in China’s tech industry, where employees work from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week.
Extension of the U.S.-China AI war
Washington has spent years restricting Chinese companies’ access to advanced Nvidia chips, and is scrutinizing their use of overseas data centers and cloud services. But no comparable restrictions prevent Chinese AI companies from establishing U.S. operations and hiring engineers there.
Both Washington and Beijing are increasingly seeking to protect their most advanced AI technologies from each other.
The Chinese government proposed export controls on some of the country’s most advanced AI models, particularly those trained using the country’s “important data,” despite specifications.
U.S. officials and American AI companies, meanwhile, have accused Chinese AI labs of using unauthorized distillation techniques to replicate their models’ capabilities. On other sensitive tech fronts, like the semiconductor industry, the U.S. has already restricted some American engineers from working in Chinese facilities without a license.
While neither country has imposed a blanket ban on AI companies hiring researchers across borders, the growing competition over advanced technology could make talent recruitment another flashpoint.
“Given it is already so competitive, it doesn’t take much to imagine U.S. companies at some point capitalizing on U.S.-China competition and making national security arguments that will make it more difficult for Chinese labs to operate or to attract the best talent. Conversely, it’d be a similar dynamic if U.S. labs were operating in China,” Ma said. “This elite talent is by definition scarce; we are talking [about] like the top 5%–10% of people. Who wouldn’t want to hoard the best and the brightest for themselves?”
Chinese tech companies have previously faced U.S. restrictions that disrupted their American research operations. In 2019, telecom giant Huawei cut more than 600 jobs at its U.S. research arm, Futurewei, after Washington placed the company on a trade blacklist.
Not all Chinese AI companies want to hire in the U.S. China’s AI poster child, DeepSeek, continues to advertise research and engineering positions in China. It recently announced about 150 positions for engineers who would expand AI agentic and back-end infrastructure. In a 2024 interview, DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng said he hired mostly Chinese-educated people and believed the company itself could cultivate elite AI researchers.
Yale researcher Wu is skeptical that Chinese startups could attract enough top researchers to compete with America’s leading AI labs. “They may have plans to hire, but that doesn’t necessarily mean they’ll be able to find the people,” she said.

India, EU resolve to boost tech and investment ties ahead of sealing of landmark trade deal
India and the 27-nation bloc are set to seal next month the landmark free trade agreement -- billed as the "mother of all deals" -- to create a market of two billion people.
NEW DELHI: Weeks ahead of inking of a mega trade pact, India and European Union (EU) on Monday vowed to boost their ties in trade and investment, quantum technologies, semiconductors and biotechnology to deliver "mutually beneficial and transformative" outcomes.
The two sides also agreed to work towards conclusion of the proposed investment protection agreement and the pact on geographical indications.
A comprehensive scrutiny of the two-way engagement was carried out at the seventh India-EU Strategic Partnership Review Meeting (SPRM) held in New Delhi.
"Both sides reviewed engagements towards boosting trade and investment cooperation, including the timely signing and implementation of the India-EU free trade agreement, and to continue work towards conclusion of the investment protection agreement and the agreement on geographical indications," according to a joint press statement.
"The discussions also covered strengthening supply chains and economic security, including strategic engagements in the Trade and Technology Council (TTC) and Blue Valleys initiative," it said.
The TTC was unveiled in 2022 to facilitate exchange of critical technologies relating to an array of domains including artificial intelligence, quantum computing, semiconductors and cybersecurity.
At the SPRM, both sides also discussed cooperation on critical and emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), quantum technologies, digital public infrastructure (DPI), advanced semiconductors, clean technologies and biotechnology.
The deliberations also saw a resolve for cooperation to advance a conducive digital environment and promote digital public infrastructure.
It said the two sides expressed satisfaction on deepening research collaboration, including India's potential association with Horizon Europe, a Euro 93.5-billion flagship research and innovation programme.
India's association with the Horizon Europe programme is seen as part the comprehensive strategic agenda of the two sides for the next five years.
"The two sides underscored the importance of strengthening connectivity partnership including Global Gateway, India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) and trilateral projects in clean energy, climate resilience, green mobility and digitalisation," the press statement noted.
"They also agreed to enhance coordination and cooperation towards shaping effective global governance," it said.
India and the EU also exchanged views on enhancing people-to-people contacts, including in the areas of talent mobility, education and skills development, as well as reviewed updates on the European Legal Gateway Office.
They also looked forward to the next edition of the India-EU Human Rights Dialogue, the statement said.
"As trusted, predictable and like-minded partners, they reaffirmed their commitment to deepen the India-EU Strategic Partnership, and to deliver mutually beneficial, concrete and transformative outcomes.
"The meeting also provided an opportunity to review preparations for future meetings at leaders' level," the statement added.
It said both sides renewed their commitments to advance the clean transition, and pursue cooperation to include Indian ship recycling yards which comply with the European Union Regulation on Ship Recycling in its list of ship recycling facilities.
The SPRM was co-chaired by Sibi George, Secretary (West) in the Ministry of External Affairs and Matti Maasikas, Deputy Secretary General for Geoeconomics and Interinstitutional Issues at the European External Action Service.

india-69d3b8c1ee.headline: Ahead of Abu Dhabi peace talks, Modi speaks to Zelenskyy; Jaishankar speaks to Lavrov
india-69d3b8c1ee.source: India Latest News: Top National Headlines Today & Breaking News | The Hindu
india-69d3b8c1ee.fulltext:
India is ready to mediate between Russia and Ukraine to establish “food corridors”, announced Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, welcoming the offer after a telephone call with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, ahead of the Ukraine-Russia peace talks set to begin in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. Mr. Modi conveyed India’s “readiness” to help with all initiatives to end the nearly five-year-old conflict. The call was followed by another call between External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, in the clearest indication thus far of the mediatory role that New Delhi is now playing between Moscow and Kyiv.
On Tuesday, U.S. President Donald Trump’s negotiators, including his son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, will restart negotiations after three months with Russian and Ukrainian representatives to discuss security guarantees required for a possible ceasefire. The calls from New Delhi came just ahead of the talks in the UAE, and a week before Mr. Modi and Mr. Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the ASEAN-linked summits in Manila. Later this month, Mr. Trump is expected to travel to Shenzhen for the APEC summit in China, that Russian President Vladimir Putin is also expected to attend, making the timing of the Modi-Zelenskyy and Jaishankar-Lavrov calls more significant.
“Prime Minister [Modi] reaffirmed India’s human-centric approach and reiterated India’s consistent position that the conflict must be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy,” the Ministry of External Affairs said in a statement about the Modi-Zelenskyy call. “He conveyed India’s readiness to contribute to all efforts aimed at peaceful resolution of the conflict,” it added.
In a post on social media, Mr. Zelenskyy said he had briefed Mr. Modi on the latest developments and stressed that Mr. Modi had said to Mr. Putin that the war must end. The Ukrainian President said Russia must understand that the “global economy and hundreds of millions of people around the world are suffering because of blocked sea routes” in the Black Sea, and called for India to clarify its peace proposal.
“It is important that India identify what steps it can take and what dialogue it can pursue with other leaders to help bring the war to an end. Food security could be one such area. We discussed Russia’s blocking of grain exports via the Black Sea. India is ready to mediate in establishing food corridors, and we are counting on these efforts to continue,” Mr. Zelenskyy wrote.
Within a couple of hours of the announcement, Mr. Jaishankar posted that he had spoken to his Russian counterpart Mr. Lavrov as well, and said their conversation had “focused on the Ukraine conflict and ongoing diplomatic initiatives”. Mr. Jaishankar, who has been discussing India’s proposals on a grain export agreement or a food corridor in the Black Sea, on the safety of sea mariners, and safe passage for energy shipments with both countries, had first disclosed the initiatives during a visit to Poland and Ukraine in September. On October 22, during the visit of Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk to Delhi, Indian officials had said it had reached out to both Russian and Ukrainian governments with a “four-point proposal” for an agreement that would stop attacks on civilians, allow grain and energy exports from both countries through the Black Sea, and end the targeting of ships and seafarers, many of whom are Indian nationals. Highly placed officials had told The Hindu that New Delhi was in close contact with both sides over the specific proposal, and the government had hoped to hear back from both the Russian and Ukrainian sides at the earliest. With talks set to begin on Tuesday, it remains to be seen whether India will join the dialogue already in play with the U.S. and the UAE, or whether New Delhi plans a larger role in mediating or hosting talks between Russia and Ukraine in the future.

world-c557d34e0b.headline: Iran was behind cyber-attack on French supermarket freezers, Paris says
world-c557d34e0b.fulltext:
France has said Iran was responsible for a massive cyber-attack on supermarket freezers and chiller cabinets that was described by its foreign minister as being an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression”.
Jean-Noël Barrot said “Europe-wide sanctions” would be imposed against those responsible, adding that the attacks – which took control of digital thermostats to push temperatures up to above 50C – constituted “a major violation of the nation’s interests”.
At a press briefing during the G7 summit in Paris, he said: “Thanks to the remarkable efforts of government agencies, I am able to confirm that the Islamic Republic of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards are responsible for this attack.”
He said the Iranian ambassador had been summoned “to protest in the strongest possible terms against this extremely serious act.”
Swathes of French supermarkets were hit in the cyber-attacks on 11 and 12 October. Some were forced to throw away entire inventories of perishable food.
Similar incidents have been reported since, including on supermarket fridges in other European countries last week and on a French blood bank.
The Paris public prosecutor, Laure Beccuau, said on Monday that specialist investigators and government agencies had identified “a modus operandi” characteristic of the Iranian group Shahid Kaveh, a cyber warfare unit linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC).
This included “the use of Farsi and IP addresses traced back to devices located in Iran”, she said.
Beccuau said her office had opened a investigation against the head of Shahid Kaveh, his deputies and “others who will be identified” on charges of “fraudulent attacks on an automated data processing system committed as part of an organised crime ring and of causing damage dangerous to persons”.
She said the offences were “aggravated by the fact they were committed to serve a foreign power – in this case Iran”.
Gérôme Billois, a partner at the cybersecurity and technology company Wavestone, said Shahid Kaveh had been active since 2020 and was known to have carried out cyber-attacks mostly on water distribution systems in the US.
“Two countries are known for this kind of attack: Iran and Russia. Given that recent cyber-attacks on supermarkets and the blood bank in France concerned freezers it is reasonable to think Iran is directly linked to both,” he said,
“For the moment they are attacking easy equipment but as a state group that has the means, the determination and the time, we should be prepared to see attacks on other systems like water or electricity.”
During the attack last month, hackers remotely overrode the temperature setting on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets in as many as 700 supermarkets and shops across France, pushing them from as low as -27C (-16.6F) to well over 50C (122F) in some cases.
Thousands of tons of food had to be dumped and in some stores the extreme temperature rise sparked fires, triggering sprinklers and water damage.
Hackers last week accessed control systems at cold stores stocking blood products. The French blood service (EFS) said temperature and defrosting thresholds and been raised to “very high level” but that technicians had been alerted by alarm systems allowing them to disconnect the cold stores before the products were destroyed. It is not clear whether the two attacks are linked.
The following day retailers in 11 European countries including the UK, Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with refrigeration systems.
A regional branch of France’s Crédit Mutuel bank also reported losing more than €100m in a cyber-attack on Friday. The bank said it had recuperated some of the money.
The European Commission did not immediately comment on the French foreign minister’s statement. Kaja Kallas, the head of foreign affairs for the EU said: “We have the foreign affairs council next Monday, so we will have the opportunity to discuss this. These cyber incidents occurring in Europe, if attributed [to Iran], also call for a strong response on our part.”
In a significant decision this year, the EU designated the IRGC a terrorist organisation, ending years of division over the issue. The designation became possible after France dropped its long-held opposition, having previously feared it would damage diplomatic channels and the interests of French nationals in Iran.
