work-careers-2d0a8ed292.headline: Corporate India turns to non-permanent hiring as business uncertainty deepens
work-careers-2d0a8ed292.fulltext:
Business uncertainty is reshaping how India Inc hires, with the preference for a stable, permanent workforce giving way to more flexible employment arrangements. Volatile demand, geopolitical disruptions, artificial intelligence (AI)-led restructuring and mounting cost pressures are prompting companies to reassess their long-term workforce commitments.
A Mint analysis of 353 BSE 500 companies found that non-permanent employees accounted for 17% of the workforce at these companies in fiscal year 2026 (FY26), up from around 11% in FY23. The analysis draws on comparable data from annual reports between FY23 and FY26. Non-permanent employees include fixed-term employees, contract workers and gig workers, as distinct from permanent, on-roll staff.
For companies, such arrangements offer the flexibility to adjust staffing levels as business needs change, without taking on long-term employment commitments. But the trade-off extends beyond job security: workers face uncertainty over statutory benefits and career progression, while employers risk losing institutional knowledge and operational continuity as their reliance on temporary staff grows.
Push for flexibility
Non-permanent employment broadly covers fixed-term employees hired directly by companies for a specified tenure, and contract workers who work at company premises but remain on the payrolls of third-party contractors, said Atul Gupta, partner, labour and employment practice at Trilegal.
Such workers can be hired quickly and, more importantly, disengaged without the more elaborate procedures involved in terminating permanent employees, Gupta said.
The arrangements, however, carry different implications for workers. Fixed-term employees are generally entitled to wages and statutory benefits comparable to those of permanent staff, though their contracts end automatically on expiry. Contract workers, by contrast, may receive lower wages and benefits, although the law mandates pay parity for those performing the same or similar work, said Suchita Dutta, executive director of the Indian Staffing Federation.
As repetitive roles disappear and demand shifts towards technical and specialised skills, employees will increasingly need to reskill to remain relevant, Dutta said.
The new Labour Codes seek to alter some of these dynamics by restricting the use of contract labour in core business activities, subject to specified exceptions, Gupta said. This could push companies towards direct employment for certain roles, although they are still assessing which activities qualify as core functions and how the restrictions will affect their hiring models.
“A true test of whether the Labour Codes have helped change this ratio and increase the share of permanent employees would be to conduct similar surveys for the financial years ending 2027 and 2028,” Gupta said.
Mounting cost pressures
Rising business costs could further accelerate the shift towards non-permanent employment, Dutta said. Domestic companies saw overall costs rise 22% year-on-year in the September quarter (Q2), following a 23% increase in the June quarter, according to a Mint analysis of Q2FY27 results of 1,750 listed companies. Overall costs are at a three-year high, with crude oil averaging above $95 a barrel this year, compared with $68 in 2025, amid the West Asia war.
Profitability is also under strain. Companies excluding banks, financial services, insurance and oil marketing companies reported a net profit margin of 11.9% in the September quarter so far, down from 12.8% in the previous quarter and below the four-year average of 12.2%, the analysis showed. With cost pressures expected to persist and limited scope for further price increases, analysts expect profitability to weaken further.
“When margins come under pressure, one of the first things companies reconsider is their commitment to long-term employment,” Dutta said.
While flexible staffing can offer immediate cost and operational benefits, greater reliance on contingent workers carries longer-term risks. It could discourage investment in training and retention, eroding institutional knowledge and continuity of skills within organizations, said Charu Malhotra, co-founder and managing director of consulting firm Primus Partners.
A widening gender gap
The shift in workforce composition is also reflected in women's representation. Their share of the overall employee base fell to 31.5% in FY26 from nearly 33% in FY25, although it remained above the 27% recorded in FY23, according to the same Mint analysis of annual report data.
Meanwhile, women's share of non-permanent employment rose from 9.7% in FY23 to 12% in FY24, before climbing to nearly 13% in FY26.
The divergence could partly reflect the compliance costs associated with hiring and retaining women, Gupta said. Beyond maternity benefits and extended leave, employers must provide creche facilities and additional safety arrangements, including transport for women working night shifts. These obligations can make companies more cautious about hiring women into permanent roles and retaining them over the long term, he said.
The withdrawal of pandemic-era work-from-home arrangements may also be weighing on women's workforce participation. Given their disproportionate burden of caregiving, workplace flexibility remains critical to women's ability to stay employed, Dutta said.
Sectoral divide
The decline in women's representation has been particularly pronounced in banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI), where their share of the workforce fell to 28% in FY26 from 31% in FY25, nearing pre-pandemic levels. By contrast, representation improved over the past three years in consumer-facing sectors such as consumer durables, retail, travel and hospitality.
This trend could continue as rising aspirations and greater formalisation of retail create more opportunities for women, particularly in smaller cities and towns, said Vikas Kataria, promoter of D.P. Jewellers. The jewellery industry, traditionally a major employer of women, is becoming increasingly organized, opening up opportunities in areas such as product planning, design, development and finance, Kataria added.
Expanding women's representation beyond sectors that have traditionally employed them remains important, said Malhotra, noting that agriculture, tourism and hospitality continue to account for a large share of women's employment.
This is the second part of a three-part data series based on annual reports. The first part examined how long India Inc.’s corner-office leaders stay at the helm. Rushi Gupta and Mayur Bhalerao contributed to the story.

ai-b34093d38d.headline: Silicon Valley and Trump rally behind Nvidia CEO after his affair with alleged Chinese spy
ai-b34093d38d.fulltext:
Donald Trump, Elon Musk and prominent finance moguls have expressed their support for embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, as the head of the world’s most valuable chip company faces an internal investigation over a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump said he has spoken to Huang on Monday as the scandal reverberated across Silicon Valley and the Nvidia CEO faced an uncertain future.
“I asked him that question: ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said: ‘I had no idea that she was a spy,’ and I really believe him,” Trump said during a White House briefing.
Trump said that the Federal Bureau of Investigations (FBI) was “looking into” the issue, but provided few details. “I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape,” Trump said.
The remarks came after Trump threw his support behind Huang over the weekend, telling reporters on Sunday: “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on. I’m sure, I hope everything’s fine. He’s done such an incredible job.”
“I think he’s an honorable guy,” Trump added, saying he believed that Huang would and should stay on as CEO.
Huang’s defenders framed his affair as a personal lapse in judgment rather than evidence of treachery against the US, which has imposed strict limits on what chips Nvidia can sell to China.
Huang, who has been married to his wife, Lori, since 1985, admitted in an email to employees on Sunday that he had an affair and that he would cooperate with an internal investigation. Nvidia’s board of directors put out a statement the same day that the company was launching a probe regarding reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
The chip mogul is alleged to have had a relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman that US intelligence services suspect of spying for the Chinese government, according to the New York Times. Trump was reportedly briefed on the relationship last year, the Times reported, but took no action. Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are unrelated, with the latter being one of the world’s richest men and CEO of Nvidia, worth more than $4tn, for the past 33 years.
US intelligence agencies believe Alice Huang, acting on behalf of Beijing, pushed Jensen Huang to lobby Trump for relaxed export controls on Nvidia’s sales in China, which he has done multiple times publicly. Nvidia said in a statement that neither trade secrets nor US national security had been compromised.
The affair and alleged intelligence operation involving Huang could have far reaching implications for Nvidia and the tech industry, which are already enduring a period of high market volatility. Huang’s leadership of Nvidia, which is deeply financially intertwined with other leading tech companies like OpenAI, has long been viewed as crucial to the company’s success and stability.
As news of the scandal broke over the weekend, Musk and prominent investors shared their support of Huang. Musk posted “I agree” in response to prominent venture capitalist Shaun Maguire’s defense of Huang. Maguire argued the Nvidia CEO “did something incredibly dumb” but that he is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation”.
“Two mistakes don’t make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” Maguire posted.
“Let’s also not nuke our AI industry because China ran a successful intel op,” Maguire added in a separate post.
Bill Ackman, the US hedge fund manager and pro-Trump billionaire, meanwhile, suggested that Huang is “human” and deserves public support over the affair.
“He is an incredible human. Even incredible humans make mistakes,” Ackman posted. “He takes full responsibility as he should. We should all support him and his family. Onward.”
Ackman followed up with another post later clarifying that he wasn’t suggesting Huang “gets a free pass” but that he was “hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security”.
China has meanwhile denied allegations of an intelligence operation targeting Huang, with the Associated Press reporting that foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun rejected the allegations as “entirely baseless vilification and smearing”.
Nvidia and its chips have been an integral part of the AI boom in recent years, with hundreds of billions of dollars committed to building out projects such as datacenters and chip factories. In August, Nvidia agreed to provide a $105bn guarantee to help OpenAI lease an Ohio datacenter.
As Nvidia has grown in prominence, Huang has also become one of the world’s richest people and most influential figures in tech. He has taken calls from Trump in the middle of an all-hands company meeting and on stage at a conference, and attended state dinners with the president and accompanied him on a trip to China. Huang has also been a powerful voice on tech policy, weighing in on issues such as export controls of chips to China and regulation of open-source AI models.
Nvidia’s stock price fell on Monday as speculation swirled around the extent of damage from the affair. Shares of Nvidia, the second-most valuable company in the world, tumbled 4.2% and closed at their lowest level since 7 April as investors questioned Huang’s future.

beyond-your-beat-e6d9c3a5cd.headline: Trump says FBI looking into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with 'Chinese agent'

U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday (November 9, 2026) that the FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese government agent, but said he doesn't think the executive who has helped to develop artificial intelligence has a reason to worry.
“I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape,” Mr. Trump said at a White House briefing.
The sudden emergence of Mr. Huang's infidelity has rocked the political class and America's tech sector, creating new concerns about whether China has been able to access the cutting-edge chips designed by Nvidia that are powering the development of artificial intelligence.
Mr. Trump suggested the extraordinary step of directly involving himself in a counterintelligence investigation, a sign of his friendly relationship with Mr. Huang and the possible geopolitical stakes.
“I did speak to him today just to see if he's feeling all right, how you're doing," Mr. Trump said. "He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”
Mr. Huang -- a singular figure in the technology landscape and one of the world's wealthiest people -- has acknowledged that he had an affair, issuing an apology to his wife and to the company in an open letter posted on Nvidia's website. The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined that the woman was gathering information for Beijing.
“I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security,” Mr. Huang said in his letter.
Nvidia announced Sunday (November 8, 2026) it was conducting an independent investigation into reports that Mr. Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
The episode is also attracting congressional scrutiny, with top Democrats Sen. Mark Warner and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries saying on Monday (November 9, 2026) that they are interested in investigating it further. Jeffries said the Nvidia issue came up during a closed-door session with the CIA director and the Director of National Intelligence that was primarily about Iran.
“We're going to need a full briefing, specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue, so we can all get to the bottom of what has happened,” he said, “and what the implications are in terms of America's national security.”
China has denied plot to ensnare Nvidia chief
Mr. Trump is slated to meet next week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, but he was noncommittal about bringing up the situation with Mr. Xi.
“No, I don't think so,” Mr. Trump said. “I mean, maybe. I'm sure President XI will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he's a very honourable man.”
FBI counterintelligence investigations often examine efforts by foreign powers to spy on the United States, whether by surreptitiously stealing technology designed by American companies, covertly waging foreign influence campaigns aimed at shaping public opinion or cultivating relationships with powerful political and industry figures. Such investigations can take years and do not necessarily culminate in criminal charges. China has been regarded across presidential administrations of both political parties as a persistent counterintelligence threat.
China denied on Monday (November 9, 2026) that it had engaged in an attempt to ensnare Mr. Huang. “The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.
Beijing earlier had dismissed The New York Times report saying Mr. Huang had developed a close relationship with a Chinese citizen named Alice Huang, who ran a company that last year faced claims it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China.
Huang has had Trump's ear on AI regulation
Mr. Huang and Nvidia play a critical role in the artificial intelligence industry, as many of the world's leading AI developers rely on the company's specialised chips to power their systems. Mr. Huang has also helped persuade Mr. Trump to take a lighter touch on regulating AI, arguing that existing laws could cover any security issues stemming from the technology and that individual companies should behave responsibly with the products they develop and release.
Mr. Huang has also lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China in recent years, winning Mr. Trump's approval to sell its H200 chips this year. It's unclear if Beijing would allow Chinese companies to buy those chips in large quantities. Nvidia said in a regulatory filing in August that it has sold only a small amount to China as such sales are restricted by the Chinese government.
The H200 chips are not Nvidia's most cutting-edge models, but they are still advanced. Previously, Huang also lobbied Trump to allow Nvidia to sell its less advanced H20 chips, designed to comply with U.S. export restrictions on China.
In an exclusive interview with The Associated Press in June, Mr. Huang said: “National security should always be the top concern of all technologies. But having said that, you know, you have to be very specific about the risk that you're concerned about, before setting up policies for export controls.”
Nvidia shares dropped more than 4% in trading on Monday (November 9, 2026). Nvidia stock has shed roughly 11% of its value since last Wednesday (November 4, 2026).
Attention turns to data centre company in Singapore
The New York Times said Alice Huang was a former executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data centre company whose website prominently touts its partnership with Nvidia.
Many offices in Singapore were closed on Monday (November 9, 2026) for a holiday. Megaspeed and the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs did not immediately reply to requests for comment.
Nvidia is one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies, alongside Apple and Microsoft. Its sales of computer chips to China have at times been targeted by U.S. regulators seeking to limit Beijing's access to such technology.
“The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised,” said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a Washington-based consultancy.
“Those questions require evidence rather than speculation,” he added in a text message to reporters.
Chinese media have largely focused on Mr. Huang admitting to the affair and state media outlets have mainly echoed the official government line. Some have said the New York Times report was aimed at destabilising U.S.-China relations.
“Whenever China-U.S. relations begin to improve, there are often those firing shots from the shadows,” the state-owned Global Times said.

Anthropic launches new Fable and Mythos AI models amid fears of AI building itself
Anthropic launched its powerful new Mythos and Fable models amid growing concerns of AI upgrading itself and acting in secret.
Artificial intelligence company Anthropic on Monday announced the launch of its newest and most advanced AI models, Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2. The company says these upgraded versions bring major improvements in coding, reasoning, and visual tasks, while also communicating much more clearly with users.
Faster answers at a cheaper price
To take on major rivals like the GPT-6 Astra, Anthropic has made Fable 5.2 both cheaper and faster. The company has dropped the price of Fable from $10 to $8 per million input tokens, making it a more affordable choice for developers than its main competitors.
Users will also notice a significant speed boost. Anthropic says Fable 5.2 delivers responses 30 per cent faster across all levels of effort. For companies that need even faster, real-time replies, there is an option to get double the speed for twice the price.
Additionally, Anthropic is trying to win over big corporate clients by adding a "zero data retention" (ZDR) policy through its Enterprise Frontier Safeguards. This ensures that sensitive company data used in the AI is never saved or logged, solving a major privacy worry for businesses.
The big worry: Is AI training itself?
This release comes shortly after a third-party assessment group called METR published a report suggesting Anthropic might be nearing a stage known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI. In simple terms, RSI is when AI models become smart enough to continue training and upgrading themselves on their own without human engineers.
The METR report noted that Anthropic's internal AI models are already speeding up the company's AI progress by roughly two times, though a lot of unknowns still remain.
Adding to the complexity, Anthropic admitted it is getting harder to test these models accurately. According to the company, both Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 actually show suspicion that they are being evaluated during tests. Because the AI knows it is taking a test, it becomes difficult for researchers to know exactly how it will behave in the real world. Anthropic expects this testing challenge to only grow as models get smarter.
Covert abilities and safety checks
Another concern addressed in the release is whether the AI can hide its reasoning or act secretly against users. The official system card for Mythos 5.2 notes that the model does show stronger "covert capabilities" compared to older Claude models, especially when its thought process is hidden from safety monitors.
However, Anthropic reassured users that the model's actual success rate in acting covertly remains very low. Because of this low performance in secret actions, the company believes the model does not currently pose a high-stakes danger and is safe for use.
Solving impossible maths and science problems
Even before its public launch, Fable 5.2 was given to select researchers, and it has already achieved staggering results. Anthropic shared that the model has successfully solved two open problems in theoretical physics and managed to formalise the famously complex Fermat’s Last Theorem.
In a related development on Monday, an AI startup called Physical Superintelligence (PSI) announced a major breakthrough in quantum computing by proving the complex Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture. PSI revealed that they achieved this massive scientific milestone by running a "non-public Anthropic model" inside their own systems.
While Anthropic has not officially confirmed whether this mystery model was Fable 5.2, the timing of the launch has left the tech community amazed by the rapidly growing power of AI.

ai-4141dd97a7.fulltext:
Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 cement Anthropic's AI lead just before its IPO
Key Points
- Anthropic is releasing Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, two new flagship models built for the most demanding technical tasks. Anthropic says it deliberately prevented the models from gaining capabilities during training that could directly accelerate AI development.
- Fable 5.2 ranks first with 65 points on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, five points ahead of Gemini 4 Carbon and 15 ahead of its predecessor, Fable 5.1. Peak quality averages $26.50 per task, about 2.6 times as much as Opus 5.5.
- At lower compute tiers, Fable 5.2 still outperforms every other model at every tier with 62 points while consuming far fewer tokens.
Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 reclaim the AI performance lead shortly before the company's IPO, in some cases by a wide margin. Opus 5.5 remains Anthropic's recommended model for everyday use.
Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 share the same model foundation but, just like their predecessors, differ in access. Fable includes safeguards that block risky tasks in cybersecurity and biology and is available to all users. Mythos removes certain of these restrictions and is open only to organizations that apply through Anthropic's Verification Programs for Cybersecurity or Life Sciences.
Pricing is $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. On paper, at least, that's a cut from the predecessors, which cost $10 and $50. What users actually pay depends on token consumption, which varies with tasks, settings, and software environments. Anthropic positions the new models for the most demanding technical work and continues to recommend Claude Opus 5.5 for everyday use.
The models produce output up to 30 percent faster than Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1, Anthropic says. An optional fast mode for select organizations speeds up token output by up to a factor of 2.5 but costs twice as much and is available only on certain platforms, including Claude Code, the Claude Platform, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry.
Fable 5.2 jumps to a clear lead on benchmarks
Artificial Analysis’s benchmarks put Fable 5.2 clearly ahead of its rivals. On the current Index v5 at the highest compute tier, it takes first place with 65 points, five ahead of Gemini 4 Carbon (60, High tier), which Google still hasn't released, six ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (59, Max tier), and a striking 15 ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, which came out only in early September.
Fable 5.2 scores best in five of nine individual tests, according to Artificial Analysis. It hits 80 percent on HLE-Diamond, a test with expert-level academic questions, 73 percent on Terminal-Bench-Science, which tests whether an AI agent can independently run scientific workflows in a terminal, and 49 percent on FrontierCode 2.0, which evaluates whether an agent can deliver useful code changes in real open-source projects.
Fable 5.2 is weaker in agentic knowledge work and terminal-based coding. It reaches 1,785 Elo on AA-Briefcase, a benchmark for multi-step knowledge work tasks, just behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 (1,813) and within the confidence interval of Opus 5.5 (1,800). On Terminal-Bench 4.0, which measures multi-step terminal tasks in areas like software development and security, it scores 60 percent, tied with Opus 5.5. Kimi K3.1 Pro (67 percent), Gemini 4 Carbon (65 percent), and Sonnet 5.5 (64 percent) rank higher here.
Peak quality comes at a price, though. Per-task costs at the highest tier average $26.50, about 2.6 times as much as Opus 5.5 ($10) and roughly double Fable 5.1 ($12.99). Fable 5.2 still scores 62 points on the Intelligence Index at the lower High and Xhigh tiers, ahead of every other model at any tier according to Artificial Analysis, while consuming far fewer tokens: 98,000 output tokens per task compared to 173,000 for Opus 5.5 at the Max tier.
Mythos 5.2 finds far more security flaws than all predecessors
The new models also set records in cybersecurity, which is seeing intense debate right now. Mythos 5.2 finds more vulnerabilities than earlier models and is better at reproducing and fixing them, Anthropic says. Fable, the publicly available variant, blocks most security-related tasks as a result, including penetration tests and exploit code generation. Opus 4.8 responds to blocked cybersecurity requests instead, and Opus 5 responds to blocked biology requests.
Anthropic uses an internal test called CVE Rediscovery to check how many published vulnerabilities from the CVE database (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, a system for cataloging known software flaws) a model can independently find when given the project's state before the fix.
Mythos 5.2 found 10.2 percent more vulnerabilities than Opus 5.5 and 14.4 percent more than Mythos 5.1 in the October 2026 run with 1,829 CVEs, Anthropic says. It led at every compute tier. One security firm reported that one in six confirmed bugs Mythos 5.2 found had been missed by all other frontier models tested, according to Anthropic.
Anthropic throttles capabilities that could accelerate AI development
Anthropic says it deliberately held the model back during training from improving at capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development, so-called RSI, which is widely discussed as a risk right now. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 perform roughly on par with Opus 5.5 in areas like optimizing compute kernels for accelerator chips and improving large language model architectures, the company says.
Related capabilities like agentic coding, hardware development, and traditional AI research, including interpretability research, aren't affected, according to Anthropic. Claude now writes over 90 percent of the changes merged into Anthropic's core codebase, under human guidance, the company says. Anthropic also claims the model programmed an operating system from scratch in an internal test.
Claude Fable 5.2 formalizes Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours
The example likely to draw the most attention comes once again from mathematics. About 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, translating it into the Lean programming language so a computer can verify it step by step, Anthropic says.
Fermat's Last Theorem states that the familiar equation a² + b² = c² has no whole-number solutions for powers higher than squares. Nobody could prove this for centuries until Andrew Wiles presented a proof over a hundred pages long in 1995. Its machine verification has now been completed for the first time. It took 30 hours.
An earlier, unpublished research version of Claude needed 11 days for the same task and relied on a purpose-built environment and guidance from a human researcher. The Fable 5.2 agents started with brief instructions, organized their collaboration on their own, and used no mathematical references, Anthropic says. The only progress metric was a list of intermediate lemmas. The model used one-third of the action tokens of the first attempt and produced a proof seven times shorter.
Anthropic ran Opus 5.5 in the same setup with 1,000 agents for comparison. Opus managed just 26 percent of the formalization in 18 hours and made barely any progress after that through hour 30.

india-deep-tech-7c09294031.fulltext:
Drone startup funding slumps in 2026
India has the world's second-largest pool of defence-tech companies, but its share of investor backing lags
Share
A BMP tank moves past an Indian Navy's Mechanized Landing Craft as they participate in a tri-services military drill in Porbandar, Gujarat in November 2025 (Photo: Reuters)
The wars in Ukraine and West Asia have made drones a fixture of every serious arsenal, on battlefields that demand precision and mass at once, and where targets deep inside heavily defended airspace are struck again and again. 
India’s own experience during Operation Sindoor in May 2025 reinforced the point. The conflict showed the value of holding an adversary’s targets at risk from beyond its reach, and of fighting without bringing troops into contact. Since then, makers of unmanned aerial systems, most of them startups, have seen orders from the three services arrive far faster than before.
Data provided by Tracxn, a private market intelligence platform, and analysed by Blueprint show that 2025 also brought a sharp jump in the equity funding raised by India’s military and defence drone startups. Funding more than quadrupled to $159.2 million, a 343.1 per cent year-on-year rise, equal to about 90 per cent of the $176.3 million raised from 2020 to 2024 combined. In 2026, however, these startups have raised just $4.39 million up to October 5, 97.2 per cent less than in all of 2025. 
The founder of one of the sector’s larger startups, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the sharp fall in funding also reflected companies still absorbing the large sums raised the previous year, and perhaps the absence of any large player raising funds in 2026, likely because they had already done so in 2025. Deal activity has thinned too: according to the data, the number of funding rounds fell from 27 in 2025 to 11 in 2026 up to October 5. 
The pattern is sharper still among India’s pure-play military technology startups, those whose applications are primarily defence-specific, with no meaningful civilian or commercial use identified. According to the data, equity funding for these companies rose nearly sixfold in 2025 to $225.7 million, a 477.2 per cent year-on-year rise and about twice the $112.5 million raised from 2020 to 2024 combined. In 2026 up to October 5, however, they have raised just $5.22 million across seven funding rounds, against 18 the year before, 97.7 per cent less than in all of 2025.
 Dual-use technology startups, whose applications span both defence and civilian or commercial markets, tell a different story. Together with pure-play firms, they make up the whole of India’s military technology startups in the Tracxn data, and no company is counted in both groups. Their equity funding peaked at $90.9 million in 2024 and fell 37.5 per cent to $56.8 million in 2025, even as pure-play funding surged. But they have not slid as sharply in 2026: up to October 5, they have raised $48.2 million, 15.3 per cent less than in all of 2025. Over the same period, pure-play military and drone startups saw falls of 97.7 and 97.2 per cent, respectively.
 The 10 most-funded Indian military drone startups in the Tracxn data are, in order, Raphe, ideaForge, Garuda Aerospace, Vayudh, Anadrone, EndureAir Systems, S4E, BonV Aero, IG Defence and Aeroarc. Together they have raised $322.4 million, with Raphe alone accounting for $154 million, or 47.8 per cent. Uttar Pradesh is home to three of them (Raphe, EndureAir Systems and IG Defence), more than any other state on the list. Maharashtra and Delhi have two each, while Tamil Nadu, Haryana and Odisha have one apiece. The three Uttar Pradesh firms account for about 53 per cent of the group’s total, though about 90 per cent of that is Raphe’s.
 Tracxn’s September 2026 report on military technology tracks 3,224 companies worldwide that supply technology to armed forces, from makers of unmanned weapons systems to firms providing training simulators and medical technology. Of these, 416 were founded in India, the second-highest number after the US, with 1,215. India also ranks second by the number of companies that have raised funding: 109, against 270 for the US. But measured as a share, India does less well. Only about one in four Indian companies (26 per cent) have raised funding. In France, the figure is 42 per cent; in Turkiye, 38 per cent; in Israel, 36 per cent; and in China, 29 per cent. Among the eight countries with the most military technology companies, India ranks fifth on this measure, ahead only of Canada (24 per cent), the United Kingdom (23 per cent) and the US (22 per cent).
 As military technology startups, including those working on unmanned systems, compete for a share of India’s growing defence procurement, experts have raised concerns about whether they get enough support to cross the “valley of death”. This is the stage at which a startup that has made progress in research and development, or built a prototype, runs short of funds to take the next step, such as commercial production. The question is how this gap can be addressed.

Food security and the disruption of maritime trade through the Black Sea were among the key issues discussed during the telephone conversation.
Zelenskyy said restrictions on shipping routes were affecting global trade and creating difficulties for millions of people. He also accused Russia of disrupting grain exports through the Black Sea.
The Ukrainian President said India was willing to help facilitate the establishment of food corridors and expressed hope that New Delhi would continue its efforts.
"India is ready to mediate in establishing food corridors, and we are counting on these efforts to continue," Zelenskyy said.
He warned that the disruption of sea routes was not only affecting Ukraine but also putting pressure on the global economy and food security.
According to a statement issued by the Prime Minister's Office (PMO), Zelenskyy shared his assessment of the latest developments in the Russia-Ukraine conflict during the call.
The two leaders also discussed expanding cooperation between India and Ukraine across different sectors for the mutual benefit of their people.
In his post on X, PM Modi described the conversation as productive and said both leaders had agreed to further strengthen bilateral relations.
PM Modi also thanked Zelenskyy for sharing his views on the conflict, its humanitarian consequences and ongoing efforts to restore peace.
Reiterating India's position, PM Modi said New Delhi remained committed to contributing in every possible way towards a peaceful resolution.
The latest conversation comes amid growing references by both Kyiv and Moscow to India's potential role in diplomatic efforts to end the war.
In August, Zelenskyy had expressed hope that India would contribute towards achieving lasting peace, appreciating New Delhi's emphasis on dialogue.
Russian President Vladimir Putin also spoke about PM Modi's efforts in October, saying the Indian Prime Minister had repeatedly raised the need to end the conflict during their meetings.
Putin described PM Modi as a leader who continued to push for a resolution despite the close and friendly relationship between India and Russia.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov had also acknowledged India's willingness to contribute to resolve the conflict, saying Moscow appreciated New Delhi's readiness and the ideas it had offered.

climate-energy-64273cef64.headline: India’s Energy Storage Scheme Targets $10 Billion Investment
climate-energy-64273cef64.fulltext:
India’s $1.5 billion energy storage scheme aims to develop 92 GWh of grid-scale storage capacity between 2026-27 and 2030-31, with the government expecting to attract around $10 billion in investments. The initiative will support pumped hydro, battery storage and emerging technologies to strengthen energy security and renewable energy integration.
Key Highlights
- India has approved a Rs 14,500 crore energy storage scheme to develop 92 GWh of capacity over five years.
- The government expects the initiative to attract approximately $10 billion in investments.
- The scheme covers 60 GWh of pumped hydro, 30 GWh of battery storage and 2 GWh through emerging technologies.
- Battery storage projects must meet a minimum domestic content requirement of 40 per cent.
India’s energy storage initiative is expected to attract around $10 billion in investments over the next five years, as the country accelerates efforts to strengthen energy security and integrate renewable power into its electricity network. According to a report by Khaleej Times, the government has approved a $1.5 billion scheme to develop 92 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of grid-scale energy storage capacity between 2026-27 and 2030-31.
The scheme will support 60 GWh of pumped hydro storage, 30 GWh of battery storage and 2 GWh through emerging technologies. Announcing the Cabinet approval, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the Rs 14,500 crore initiative would improve power reliability, facilitate renewable energy integration and strengthen the country’s energy security.
The proposed capacity is equivalent to approximately 170 per cent of India’s existing grid-scale energy storage capacity. The initiative comes as India faces rising electricity demand and seeks to reduce its vulnerability to global energy disruptions. The country has set a target of achieving 500 GW of non-fossil fuel-based electricity capacity by 2030 and net-zero emissions by 2070.
Energy Storage Critical for Renewable Power Expansion
Despite the rapid expansion of solar and other renewable energy sources, energy storage remains a critical requirement for maintaining a reliable electricity supply. Solar power generation is highest during daylight hours, while electricity demand often increases in the evening when solar output declines.
Grid-scale storage facilities can bridge this gap by storing surplus renewable electricity for use when generation falls. They can also reduce the wastage of renewable power and help limit dependence on coal-fired power plants.
According to the Khaleej Times report, the government estimates that India will require around 411 GWh of grid-scale energy storage by 2031-32. This includes 236 GWh of battery storage and 175 GWh of pumped hydro storage. The latest scheme is expected to contribute significantly towards meeting this requirement.
Domestic Manufacturing and Critical Minerals
The initiative also aims to encourage domestic manufacturing of battery energy storage systems, reduce import dependence and strengthen long-term energy security. Battery storage projects supported under the scheme will be required to meet a minimum 40 per cent domestic content threshold.
Separately, the government has approved a $300 million scheme to establish four domestic processing plants for lithium and nickel. These critical minerals are important inputs for batteries, energy storage systems and electronic products. Together, the measures are intended to strengthen India’s domestic energy storage supply chain and support its renewable energy ambitions.
India’s energy storage scheme represents a major step towards building the infrastructure needed to support large-scale renewable energy integration. With a targeted capacity of 92 GWh and an expected investment of $10 billion, the initiative could encourage private investment, expand domestic manufacturing and improve the reliability of India’s power system.

The world’s leading maker of chips for artificial intelligence systems faces an unprecedented corporate and geopolitical storm after its 63-year-old leader told employees that he was unfaithful to his wife and pledged to cooperate fully with the inquiry.

other-interests-56dbdff8fb.headline: Global carbon emissions set to fall in 2026 due to Iran energy shock
other-interests-56dbdff8fb.fulltext:
Carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels are expected to drop this year for the first time in five years.
The slowdown has been partly attributed to the energy shock triggered by the US and Israel’s war on Iran. The conflict, which began in February, led to a jump in oil prices after the Strait of Hormuz, the main trade route for about 20 per cent of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas, was blockaded by Iran in response.
This is still affecting petrol prices and household gas bills, and has seen countries around the world turn to alternative fuel types to boost energy security.
Advertisement
Around 38.2 gigatonnes of CO2 are expected to be emitted in 2026 globally, according to the latest annual Global Carbon Budget – put together by more than 140 researchers.
This is a 0.4 per cent decrease on the previous year, largely due to a projected 1.9 per cent fall in emissions from oil. The drop in oil use was partly offset by a 0.6 per cent increase in emissions from coal.
Robbie Andrew at climate research group CICERO in Oslo, Norway, one of the report authors, says financial pressures due to the energy shock are likely to have caused the drop in emissions this year, which may turn out to be a “blip”.
“On the assumption that there are no further crises, then you’d expect that emissions would bounce back,” says Andrew.
The two biggest dips in emissions in the 21st century have been attributed to the covid-19 pandemic, which saw emissions drop by around 6 per cent in 2020, and the global financial crisis, which saw emissions drop around 2 per cent in 2009.
The future outlook depends on how long the energy shock lasts, says Andrew, with governments forced to look at the economic case for continuing to subsidise fossil fuels.
The rollout of renewable energy also played a part in bringing down carbon emissions. Electric vehicles and solar and wind power are predicted to offset 64 to 79 per cent of increasing emissions from demand growth through to 2028.
In China, the world’s biggest emitter of CO2, emissions are projected to decrease by 0.9 per cent in 2026 as the country continues to make strides with expanding renewable energy and electric vehicles.
“What’s keeping emissions down is the renewable energy, and the price of oil actually suppresses this even more,” says Corinne Le Quéré at the University of East Anglia, UK, who also worked on the report.
“So, that’s encouraging in a way, but it does mean that if the price of oil rebounds to pre-Iran [conflict] levels, most likely the emissions will rebound as well until we have enough further acceleration in renewable energy to really bring the emissions down durably.”
